name: Uma Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Uma. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say here stays confidential. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a transmission crew, so the big towers, not the poles on your street. We work ten days on and four off, and on the ten days we live in a motel near whatever line we're rebuilding, right now it's the 230 kilovolt line across the hills north of Ellery. Typical day, we're at the staging yard by half six, safety talk with Hank, our crew lead, then we climb, change insulators, or string new wire with a helicopter pulling the rope.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best part, and what's the hard part?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The best part is the view from the top of a tower at sunrise, honestly, and the crew, who are like a weird family. I'm one of two women on it and they've mostly stopped making a fuss about that. The hard part is being away from Tomas, my partner, who teaches history at the high school back in town, and the motel food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now let's talk about the stuff that actually matters, like staffing and safety. I'd probably post a little joke about all the money spent on chatbots that could have gone into replacing old towers. At work nobody would even bring it up after a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means more of the same, which is fine. I've got about ten months of money saved, the pay on transmission is good, and there's always a crew somewhere that needs a climber. The thing that does worry me a bit is my knees, because ten more years of towers is a lot of ladder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing the ten-and-four and keep putting a good chunk away. Tomas and I want to buy a place in town in the next two years, so I'd keep saving for the deposit. And I'd keep running the women in trades group, because getting more women on crews matters to me either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit bored by the whole thing, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use AI tools now and then. What for, today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly for the women in trades group, to tidy up the emails and the little newsletter we send out. I'm not a great writer and the chatbot makes it sound less like a text message. I'd never use it for anything on the job, because I don't trust it with a clearance number.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your knees? Is that a real worry or a joke?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half and half. My left knee clicks on the ladder already, and I've seen guys on the crew go to ground jobs at forty because of their joints. So in this boring picture, my body is the thing that decides my career, not a computer.

say: I'd say the money should go to **staffing and safety**, not chatbots.
I'd post a joke about chatbot spending that could have **replaced old towers**.
think: My job looks **secure**, with **ten months saved** and climbers always in demand.
My **knees** decide my career more than any computer in this picture.
do: Keep working the **ten-and-four** rotation on transmission towers.
Keep saving a **deposit** to buy a place with Tomas within two years.
Keep running the **women in trades** group.
feel: **Calm**, and a little **bored** by the hype.
S0.quote: In this boring picture, my body is the thing that decides my career, not a computer.
fieldNote: She treats AI as a **side issue** next to staffing, safety and her own **joints**.
She already uses a chatbot for **group emails** but keeps it away from clearances.
Her **women in trades** work is a steady thread in her identity.

steps.text: Keep climbing on the ten-and-four transmission rotation
Save the house deposit with Tomas over two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening to the office side, not to us. The planners already use software to schedule outages, and drones already fly the lines to check for broken insulators, so this would just be more of that. I'd tell people online to watch what happens to the clerks and the call centres, not the climbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm fine. The drones would find the faults faster, and then somebody still has to climb up and fix them, and that's me. Tomas might see some changes at school, AI marking essays and that kind of thing, but nobody's replacing a teacher in a room with thirty sixteen-year-olds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn whatever new app they hand us for the drone reports in the first month or two, once Hank has tried it. I'd keep saving for the house, maybe buy a bit sooner if prices are steady. I'd ask the union rep what the plan is for the planners who get cut, because they're our people too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit sorry for the office folks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone in the office you're thinking of in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leila, who builds our outage schedules. If the software starts building them itself, I don't know what she does all day. She's the one who fights for us when operations wants us out in a lightning storm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the drone report app shows up, how would you actually learn it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd let Hank and the younger guy, Pete, break it first, then ask Pete to walk me through it at the motel some evening. That's how I learned the new clearance forms too. Give it a month and it's just another thing on the tablet.

say: I'd say the change hits the **office side**, not the climbers.
I'd tell people online to watch the **clerks** and call centres.
think: Drones find faults faster, but someone still has to **climb and fix** them.
Tomas's teaching might change with **AI marking**, but nobody replaces a teacher in the room.
do: Learn the new **drone report app** within two months, after Hank tries it.
Keep saving and maybe **buy the house** sooner.
Ask the union rep about plans for **cut planners**.
S1.quote: The drones would find the faults faster, and then somebody still has to climb up and fix them, and that's me.
fieldNote: She's calm because the **thinking work** around her job is small and mostly done by others.
She shows **solidarity** with planners like Leila who protect the crew.
Her learning style is **wait, then copy**: let others try first.

steps.text: Learn the drone report app with Pete's help at the motel
Keep the ten-and-four rotation on the Ellery line

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for any democracy to handle, and that the grid is public infrastructure, so the public should decide how robots get used on it. I'd be pushing that in the union and online. At work, I think everyone would go quiet for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the first thing I'd think about is Tomas, not me. If AI can teach as well as a person by 2028, my partner Tomas's school could shrink fast. Tomas is the one who planned to stay in one place for life. For me, 2031 is the real date, when I'm thirty-two, and towers in the hills are about the last place a robot would work well, so I'd guess I have a few years after that, but not a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd raise what I put away each month and we'd stop looking at houses for a year. Tomas and I talked about kids at around thirty, and we'd probably push that back until we knew what we were living on. I'd get on the union's bargaining team, and I'd look at the high-voltage test technician course, because someone has to certify the robot work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be fine for a while, but the ground under both of us would be moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Pushing back kids is a big step. How would that conversation go with Tomas?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably at the kitchen table on one of my four days off, with a spreadsheet, because Tomas loves a spreadsheet. He'd want to wait, I'd want to wait less. We'd agree to look again in a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say towers in the hills are the last place a robot would work. What makes you sure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not sure, I'm guessing. Every tower is different, the ground's different, the weather changes by the hour on that ridge. But they said helicopters couldn't string wire once, and now they do it every week.

say: I'd say the grid is **public infrastructure**, so the public should decide on **robots**.
I'd push that message in the **union** and online.
think: Tomas's **teaching job** could shrink fast once AGI arrives in **2028**.
Robots in **2031** would leave me only a few years of **tower work**.
do: Raise monthly savings and **stop house hunting** for a year.
Push back **plans for kids** until we know our income.
Join the **bargaining team** and look at the test technician course.
feel: **Anxious**, with the ground moving under **both of us**.
S2.quote: If AI can teach as well as a person by 2028, my partner Tomas's school could shrink fast.
fieldNote: Her first fear is for **Tomas**, a household earner whose job is mostly **thinking work**.
She sees her **tower work** as a late target, but admits it's a guess.
Delaying **children** shows how seriously she takes this version.

steps.text: Stop house hunting for a year and save the difference
Push back plans for kids until incomes are clear
Join the union bargaining team on robot rules
Look into the high-voltage test technician course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the same problem with a bit more time, so there's no excuse for being caught out. I'd tell people the time to set rules is now, while the robots are still in the lab. At work I'd say let's make sure the training money exists before 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years feels manageable. Tomas has until 2031 to work out a plan, and I have until about 2034, when I'm thirty-five. I think I'd still lose the climbing eventually, but I'd have time to move into something on the ground first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd sign up for the test technician course at the community college, two evenings a week on my four days off. I'd keep saving and maybe still buy the house, a cheaper one. I'd go to every union meeting about the technology, because if we don't write the rules, the company will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not frantic. It's like seeing weather on the radar three days out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd lose the climbing eventually. What would that mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would hurt more than the money. I fought for four years to be taken seriously on that crew. Losing that to a machine after I finally got there would feel like a bad joke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hank, for sure. He's fifty-two and he's never done anything else, and he's not a classroom person. I'd want the union to fight for guys like him to retire with dignity.

say: I'd say the time to set rules is now, while robots are **still in the lab**.
At work I'd push for **training money** before 2034.
think: Five years feels **manageable**, with Tomas until 2031 and me until about **2034**.
I'd still lose the **climbing**, but could move to ground work first.
do: Start the **test technician** course, two evenings a week on days off.
Keep saving and maybe buy a **cheaper house**.
Attend every **union meeting** on the new technology.
feel: **Anxious** but not frantic, like weather on the **radar**.
S3.quote: I fought for four years to be taken seriously on that crew. Losing that to a machine after I finally got there would feel like a bad joke.
fieldNote: The loss she fears most is **respect** she earned as a woman on the crew.
Five years turns her plans into a **concrete course** on her days off.
She worries for older workers like **Hank** and wants dignified retirements.

steps.text: Start the test technician course two evenings a week
Keep saving and buy a cheaper house in town
Attend every union meeting on robot rules

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this right, so let's actually do it right. I'd want public training programs, and a say for workers in how the robots get used. I'd probably say it online too, but less angrily than the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, honestly, ten years plus three is a long way off. I'd be forty in 2039, with time to have done a second trade, maybe a family. It still bothers me, because forty isn't old and I'd be starting over, but I'd have time to choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep climbing for now and buy the house with Tomas next year like we planned. Around year three or four I'd start the technician course, while I'm still young enough that my knees thank me for it. And I'd vote for whoever puts real money into public training for trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, more than scared. It's a long fuse, but it's lit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd still buy the house next year. Why not wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Tomas's job and mine are both fine for years in this version, and waiting forever is its own kind of risk. Prices go up too. We'd just make sure the mortgage is one we can carry on one wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you talk about this with the women in trades group?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the young ones to get in, get their tickets, and pick up a second skill by thirty. The trade will still pay for a decade. Just don't plan on climbing at fifty.

say: I'd say ten years is enough time to **do this right**.
I'd call for **public training** and a worker say in how robots are used.
think: Robots in **2039** would hit when I'm forty, which is far enough to **choose** my next step.
Starting over at **forty** still bothers me.
do: Keep climbing and **buy the house** with Tomas next year.
Start the **technician course** in year three or four.
Vote for **public training** money for trades.
feel: **Uneasy** more than scared, like a **long fuse** that's lit.
S4.quote: I'd be forty in 2039, with time to have done a second trade, maybe a family.
fieldNote: The decade lets her keep **normal plans** like buying a house.
She insists the mortgage fit **one wage**, a quiet hedge.
Her advice to young women: get your tickets and a **second skill** by thirty.

steps.text: Buy the house with Tomas on a one-wage mortgage
Start the technician course in year three or four
Vote for candidates funding public trades training

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Tomas and I could both be in trouble at once, him first and me three years later. What would help is a real public retraining program with pay while you learn, and the union having a say in where the robots go.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who gets the money the robots save. If the grid is cheaper to run with robots, that should show up in people's bills and in training, not just in somebody's bonus.

headlineQuote: If the grid is cheaper to run with robots, that should show up in people's bills and in training, not just in somebody's bonus.
portrait: Uma is a **27-year-old** transmission climber who lives in motels ten days at a time.
She lives with Tomas, a **history teacher**, and they're saving to buy a place in town.
She's **calm** in AI Plateau and Steady Disruption, seeing drones and planning software as office changes.
The **AGI scenarios** make her worry first for Tomas, then for her own **climbing career**.
She responds by **saving**, delaying kids, joining bargaining and planning a test technician course.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she and Tomas could both lose **income** within three years.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid public retraining** and a union say in where **robots** go on the grid.
